"""Implements run-time assertions.

These are Mojo built-ins, so you don't need to import them.
"""

from std._plugin import CurrentPlugin
from std.format._utils import _FixedWriteBuffer
from std.io.io import _printf
from std.os import abort
from std.sys import (
    is_apple_gpu,
    is_gpu,
)
from std.sys._build import is_debug_build
from std.sys.intrinsics import assume
from std.sys.defines import get_defined_string
from std.collections.string.string_span import _get_kgen_string
from std.reflection import call_location, SourceLocation

comptime ASSERT_MODE = get_defined_string["ASSERT", "safe"]()
"""The compile-time assertion mode from the ASSERT environment variable."""

comptime _NO_MESSAGE = "assertion failed"
"""Must remain a string literal: the no-message path passes `byte_length() + 1`
and relies on the trailing nul in static memory."""


@inline(.nodebug)
def _string_free_comptime_assert[
    cond: Bool, msg: StaticString, *extra: StaticString
]():
    """Compile-time assertion that avoids `String` to prevent circular deps.

    This exists because `debug_assert` cannot use `comptime assert` with
    `String`-based messages — `String` transitively depends on `debug_assert`,
    which would create infinite recursion in the parameter domain.
    """

    __mlir_op.`kgen.param.assert`[
        cond=cond.__mlir_bool__(),
        message=_get_kgen_string[msg, *extra](),
    ]()


@inline(.never)
def _assert_enabled[assert_mode: StaticString, cpu_only: Bool]() -> Bool:
    _string_free_comptime_assert[
        ASSERT_MODE == "none"
        or ASSERT_MODE == "warn"
        or ASSERT_MODE == "safe"
        or ASSERT_MODE == "all",
        "-D ASSERT=",
        ASSERT_MODE,
        " but must be one of: none, warn, safe, all",
    ]()
    _string_free_comptime_assert[
        assert_mode == "none" or assert_mode == "safe",
        "assert_mode=",
        assert_mode,
        " but must be one of: none, safe",
    ]()

    # FIXME: Enable assertions on Apple GPU after MOCO-2405 is fixed
    comptime if ASSERT_MODE == "none" or (
        is_gpu() and cpu_only
    ) or is_apple_gpu():
        return False
    elif ASSERT_MODE == "all" or ASSERT_MODE == "warn" or is_debug_build():
        return True
    else:
        return ASSERT_MODE == assert_mode


@inline(.never)
def _debug_assert_fail_format[
    *Ts: Writable
](location: SourceLocation, *messages: *Ts):
    var message = _FixedWriteBuffer()

    comptime for i in range(messages.__len__()):
        messages[i].write_to(message)

    var cstr = message.nul_terminate()
    var bytes_with_nul = cstr.as_bytes_with_nul()
    _debug_assert_msg(
        bytes_with_nul.unsafe_ptr(), len(bytes_with_nul), location
    )


@inline(.always)
def _debug_assert_fail[*Ts: Writable](*messages: *Ts, location: SourceLocation):
    """Reports a failed assertion, formatting the message if there is one."""

    comptime if messages.__len__() == 0:
        _debug_assert_msg(
            _NO_MESSAGE.ptr(), _NO_MESSAGE.byte_length() + 1, location
        )
    else:
        _debug_assert_fail_format(location, *messages)


@inline(.always)
def debug_assert[
    Cond: def() -> Bool,
    assert_mode: StaticString = "none",
    *Ts: Writable,
    cpu_only: Bool = False,
](cond: Cond, *messages: *Ts, location: Optional[SourceLocation] = None):
    """Asserts that the condition is true at run time.

    If the condition is false, the assertion displays the given message and
    causes the program to exit.

    You can pass in multiple arguments to generate a formatted
    message. No string allocation occurs unless the assertion is triggered.

    ```mojo
    var x = 0
    debug_assert(x > 0, "expected x to be more than 0 but got: ", x)
    ```

    Normal assertions are off by default—they only run when the program is
    compiled with all assertions enabled. You can set the `assert_mode` to
    `safe` to create an assertion that's on by default:

    ```mojo
    var x = 0
    debug_assert[assert_mode="safe"](
        x > 0, "expected x to be more than 0 but got: ", x
    )
    ```

    Use the `ASSERT` variable to turn assertions on or off when building or
    running a Mojo program:

    ```sh
    mojo -D ASSERT=all main.mojo
    ```

    The `ASSERT` variable takes the following values:

    - all: Turn on all assertions.
    - safe: Turn on "safe" assertions only. This is the default.
    - none: Turn off all assertions, for performance at the cost of safety.
    - warn: Turn on all assertions, but print any errors instead of exiting.

    To ensure that you have no run-time penalty from your assertions even when
    they're disabled, make sure there are no side effects in your message and
    condition expressions. For example:

    ```mojo
    var person = "name: john, age: 50"
    var name = "john"
    debug_assert(String("name: ", name) in person, "unexpected name")
    ```

    This will have a run-time penalty due to allocating a `String` in the
    condition expression, even when assertions are disabled. To avoid this, pass
    the condition as a closure so it runs only when the assertion is turned on:

    ```mojo
    def main():
        var person = "name: john, age: 50"
        var name = "john"

        def check_name() {name, person} -> Bool:
            return String("name: ", name) in person

        debug_assert(check_name, "unexpected name")
    ```

    If you need to allocate, and so don't want the assert to ever run on GPU,
    you can set it to CPU only:

    ```mojo
    def main():
        var person = "name: john, age: 50"
        var name = "john"

        def check_name() {name, person} -> Bool:
            return String("name: ", name) in person

        debug_assert[cpu_only=True](check_name, "unexpected name")
    ```

    For compile-time assertions, see [`comptime
    assert`](/docs/manual/metaprogramming/constraints/#compile-time-assertions)

    Parameters:
        Cond: The type of the closure to invoke to check if the assertion holds.
        assert_mode: Determines when the assert is turned on.
            - default ("none"): Turned on when compiled with `-D ASSERT=all`.
            - "safe": Turned on by default.
        Ts: The element types for the message arguments.
        cpu_only: If true, only run the assert on CPU.

    Args:
        cond: The closure to invoke to check if the assertion holds.
        messages: A set of [`Writable`](/docs/std/format/Writable/)
            arguments to convert to a `String` message.
        location: Source location to report on assertion failure.
    """

    comptime if _assert_enabled[assert_mode, cpu_only]():
        if cond():
            return

        # `debug_assert` is used a lot, so its body must generate short, concise
        # code. Avoid standard library functions that contain error/abort code
        # inside; those cause code bloat at every call site.
        #
        # `call_location()` must be resolved here rather than in the callee, so
        # that the reported location stays at this assert's own caller.
        _debug_assert_fail(
            *messages, location=location.or_else(call_location())
        )


@inline(.always)
def debug_assert[
    assert_mode: StaticString = "none",
    *Ts: Writable,
    cpu_only: Bool = False,
    _use_compiler_assume: Bool = False,
](cond: Bool, *messages: *Ts, location: Optional[SourceLocation] = None):
    """Asserts that the condition is true at run time.

    If the condition is false, the assertion displays the given message and
    causes the program to exit.

    You can pass in multiple arguments to generate a formatted
    message. No string allocation occurs unless the assertion is triggered.

    ```mojo
    var x = 0
    debug_assert(x > 0, "expected x to be more than 0 but got: ", x)
    ```

    Normal assertions are off by default—they only run when the program is
    compiled with all assertions enabled. You can set the `assert_mode` to
    `safe` to create an assertion that's on by default:

    ```mojo
    var x = 0
    debug_assert[assert_mode="safe"](
        x > 0, "expected x to be more than 0 but got: ", x
    )
    ```

    Use the `ASSERT` variable to turn assertions on or off when building or
    running a Mojo program:

    ```sh
    mojo -D ASSERT=all main.mojo
    ```

    The `ASSERT` variable takes the following values:

    - all: Turn on all assertions.
    - safe: Turn on "safe" assertions only. This is the default.
    - none: Turn off all assertions, for performance at the cost of safety.
    - warn: Turn on all assertions, but print any errors instead of exiting.

    To ensure that you have no run-time penalty from your assertions even when
    they're disabled, make sure there are no side effects in your message and
    condition expressions. For example:

    ```mojo
    var person = "name: john, age: 50"
    var name = "john"
    debug_assert(String("name: ", name) in person, "unexpected name")
    ```

    This will have a run-time penalty due to allocating a `String` in the
    condition expression, even when assertions are disabled. To avoid this, pass
    the condition as a closure so it runs only when the assertion is turned on:

    ```mojo
    def main():
        var person = "name: john, age: 50"
        var name = "john"

        def check_name() {name, person} -> Bool:
            return String("name: ", name) in person

        debug_assert(check_name, "unexpected name")
    ```

    If you need to allocate, and so don't want the assert to ever run on GPU,
    you can set it to CPU only:

    ```mojo
    def main():
        var person = "name: john, age: 50"
        var name = "john"

        def check_name() {name, person} -> Bool:
            return String("name: ", name) in person

        debug_assert[cpu_only=True](check_name, "unexpected name")
    ```

    For compile-time assertions, see [`comptime
    assert`](/docs/manual/metaprogramming/constraints/#compile-time-assertions)

    Parameters:
        assert_mode: Determines when the assert is turned on.
            - default ("none"): Turned on when compiled with `-D ASSERT=all`.
            - "safe": Turned on by default.
        Ts: The element types for the message arguments.
        cpu_only: If true, only run the assert on CPU.
        _use_compiler_assume: If true, assume the condition is true for repeated checks,
            to help the compiler optimize (default False).


    Args:
        cond: The bool value to assert.
        messages: A set of [`Writable`](/docs/std/format/Writable/)
            arguments to convert to a `String` message.
        location: Source location to report on assertion failure.
    """

    comptime if _assert_enabled[assert_mode, cpu_only]():
        if cond:
            return

        # See the sibling overload: avoid stdlib functions carrying error/abort
        # code, and resolve `call_location()` here rather than in the callee.
        _debug_assert_fail(
            *messages, location=location.or_else(call_location())
        )

    elif _use_compiler_assume:
        assume(cond)


# The two no-message overloads below omit `location` on purpose: they are
# optimized for fast compile time, because they are used frequently. An
# `Optional[SourceLocation]` and an `or_else` call generate extra IR and thus
# slow compilation down.
@inline(.always)
def debug_assert[
    Cond: def() -> Bool,
    assert_mode: StaticString = "none",
    cpu_only: Bool = False,
](cond: Cond):
    """Asserts that the condition is true at run time, with no message.

    On failure this reports `assertion failed` at the call site. Use the
    overload taking `messages` to report a formatted message instead.

    ```mojo
    def main():
        var x = 1

        def check() {x} -> Bool:
            return x > 0

        debug_assert(check)
    ```

    Parameters:
        Cond: The type of the closure to invoke to check if the assertion holds.
        assert_mode: Determines when the assert is turned on.
        cpu_only: If true, only run the assert on CPU.

    Args:
        cond: The closure to invoke to check if the assertion holds.
    """

    comptime if _assert_enabled[assert_mode, cpu_only]():
        if cond():
            return

        _debug_assert_fail(location=call_location())


@inline(.always)
def debug_assert[
    assert_mode: StaticString = "none",
    cpu_only: Bool = False,
    _use_compiler_assume: Bool = False,
](cond: Bool):
    """Asserts that the condition is true at run time, with no message.

    On failure this reports `assertion failed` at the call site. Use the
    overload taking `messages` to report a formatted message instead.

    ```mojo
    var x = 1
    debug_assert(x > 0)
    ```

    Parameters:
        assert_mode: Determines when the assert is turned on.
        cpu_only: If true, only run the assert on CPU.
        _use_compiler_assume: If true, assume the condition is true for repeated
            checks, to help the compiler optimize (default False).

    Args:
        cond: The bool value to assert.
    """

    comptime if _assert_enabled[assert_mode, cpu_only]():
        if cond:
            return

        _debug_assert_fail(location=call_location())
    elif _use_compiler_assume:
        assume(cond)


@inline(.always)
def debug_assert[
    assert_mode: StaticString = "none",

    _use_compiler_assume: Bool = False,

    """Asserts that the condition is true at run time.

    causes the program to exit.

    You can pass in multiple arguments to generate a formatted
    message. No string allocation occurs unless the assertion is triggered.

    The `ASSERT` variable takes the following values:

    - all: Turn on all assertions.
    - safe: Turn on "safe" assertions only. This is the default.

    - warn: Turn on all assertions, but print any errors instead of exiting.

    ```mojo

            return String("name: ", name) in person

    ```

    If you need to allocate, and so don't want the assert to ever run on GPU,
    you can set it to CPU only:

    ```mojo
    def main():

        var name = "john"

        def check_name() {name, person} -> Bool:
            return String("name: ", name) in person

        debug_assert[cpu_only=True](check_name, "unexpected name")
    ```

    For compile-time assertions, see [`comptime
    assert`](/docs/manual/metaprogramming/constraints/#compile-time-assertions)

    Parameters:
        assert_mode: Determines when the assert is turned on.
            - default ("none"): Turned on when compiled with `-D ASSERT=all`.
            - "safe": Turned on by default.
        cpu_only: If true, only run the assert on CPU.
        _use_compiler_assume: If true, assume the condition is true for repeated checks,
            to help the compiler optimize (default False).

    Args:
        cond: The bool value to assert.
        message: A static string message.
    """

    comptime if _assert_enabled[assert_mode, cpu_only]():
        if cond:
            return

        _debug_assert_msg(
            message.ptr(),
            # include StringLiteral null terminator for printf statements
            message.byte_length() + 1,
            call_location(),
        )
    elif _use_compiler_assume:
        assume(cond)


@inline(.never)
def _debug_assert_msg(
    message: ImmPointer[Byte, _], length: Int, loc: SourceLocation
):
    """Aborts with (or prints) the given message and location.

    This function is intentionally marked as no_inline to reduce binary size.

    Note that it's important that this function doesn't get inlined; otherwise,
    an indirect recursion of @inline(.always) functions is possible (e.g. because
    abort's implementation could use debug_assert)
    """

    # The `else` branch is required (not just for clarity): its `_printf`
    # paths recurse via `Optional.value()` → `debug_assert`. `comptime if
    # X: return` does not elide unconditional post-return code, so the
    # fallback must live in `else:` to be comptime-elided when a plugin
    # owns emission.
    comptime if CurrentPlugin._handles_debug_assert:
        CurrentPlugin.debug_assert_emit_fn(message, length, loc)
        comptime if ASSERT_MODE != "warn":
            abort()
        return
    else:
        if __is_run_in_comptime_interpreter:
            print("At: ", loc, ": Assert Error: ", message, sep="")

            comptime if ASSERT_MODE != "warn":
                abort()
            return

        _printf["At: %s:%llu:%llu: Assert Error: %s\n"](
            loc.file_name().as_c_string_span(),
            loc.line(),
            loc.column(),
            message,
        )

        comptime if ASSERT_MODE != "warn":
            abort()

"""Implements slice.

These are Mojo built-ins, so you don't need to import them.
"""

from std.format._utils import FormatStruct, Named


struct Slice(
    Equatable,
    ImplicitlyCopyable,
    Writable,
):
    """Represents a slice expression.

    Objects of this type are generated when slice syntax is used within square
    brackets, for example:

    ```mojo
    var lst: List[Int] = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]

    # Both produce the same new list: [6, 7].
    var l1 = List(lst[6:])
    var l2 = lst.__getitem__(Slice(6, len(lst)))
    ```
    """

    # Fields
    var start: Optional[Int]
    """The starting index of the slice."""
    var end: Optional[Int]
    """The end index of the slice."""
    var step: Optional[Int]
    """The step increment value of the slice."""

    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#
    # Life cycle methods
    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(out self, start: Int, end: Int):
        """Constructs a slice with the given start and end bounds.

        Args:
            start: The starting index of the slice.
            end: The end index of the slice.
        """
        self.start = start
        self.end = end
        self.step = None

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(
        out self,
        start: Optional[Int],
        end: Optional[Int],
        step: Optional[Int],
        __slice_literal__: NoneType = None,
    ):
        """Constructs a slice with the given start, end, and step values.

        Args:
            start: The starting index of the slice.
            end: The end index of the slice.
            step: The step increment value of the slice.
            __slice_literal__: Enables slice literal syntax.
        """
        self.start = start
        self.end = end
        self.step = step

    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#
    # Trait implementations
    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#

    @inline(.never)
    def write_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the slice's string representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        FormatStruct(writer, "Slice").fields(self.start, self.end, self.step)

    @inline(.never)
    def write_repr_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the slice's debug representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        FormatStruct(writer, "Slice").fields(
            Named("start", self.start),
            Named("end", self.end),
            Named("step", self.step),
        )

    @inline(.always)
    def __eq__(self, other: Self) -> Bool:
        """Compare this slice to the other.

        Args:
            other: The slice to compare to.

        Returns:
            True if start, end, and step values of this slice match the
            corresponding values of the other slice and False otherwise.
        """
        return (
            self.start == other.start
            and self.end == other.end
            and self.step == other.step
        )

    def indices(self, length: Int) -> Tuple[Int, Int, Int]:
        """Resolves the slice's bounds against the length of a container.

        Uses the target container length to resolve negative, out-of-bounds,
        or `None` bounds.

        A negative bound counts back from the end of the container:
        ```mojo
        var s = slice(0, -1, 1)
        print(s.indices(5))  # (0, 4, 1)
        ```

        A `None` bound becomes the start or the end of the container based
        on the direction of the step:
        ```mojo
        var s = slice(None, None, 1)
        print(s.indices(5))  # (0, 5, 1)
        ```

        An out-of-bounds bound is clamped to the nearest valid bound in the
        step's direction:
        ```mojo
        var s = slice(20)
        print(s.indices(5))  # (0, 5, 1)
        ```

        Args:
            length: The length of the container the slice applies to.

        Returns:
            A tuple of the resolved start, end, and step.
        """
        var step = self.step.or_else(1)

        var positive_step = step > 0

        var start: Int
        match self.start:
            case .None:
                start = 0 if positive_step else length - 1
            case .Some(s) if s < 0:
                start = s + length
                if start < 0:
                    start = 0 if positive_step else -1
            case .Some(s) if s >= length:
                start = length if positive_step else length - 1
            case .Some(s):
                start = s

        var end: Int
        match self.end:
            case .None:
                end = length if positive_step else -1
            case .Some(e) if e < 0:
                end = e + length
                if end < 0:
                    end = 0 if positive_step else -1
            case .Some(e) if e >= length:
                end = length if positive_step else length - 1
            case .Some(e):
                end = e

        return (start, end, step)


struct StridedSlice(ImplicitlyCopyable, Writable):
    """Represents a slice expression that has a stride.

    This type is used to support different behavior for strided vs unstrided
    slicing.
    """

    var _inner: Slice

    @implicit
    def __init__(out self, other: Slice):
        """Implicitly convert from a general slice.

        Args:
            other: The other slice.
        """
        self._inner = other

    def __init__(
        out self,
        start: Optional[Int],
        end: Optional[Int],
        stride: Int,
        __slice_literal__: NoneType = None,
    ):
        """Constructs a strided slice with the given start, end, and stride.

        Args:
            start: The starting index of the slice.
            end: The end index of the slice.
            stride: The step increment value of the slice.
            __slice_literal__: Enables slice literal syntax.
        """

        self._inner = Slice(start, end, stride)

    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#
    # Trait implementations
    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#

    @inline(.never)
    def write_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the strided slice's string representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        self._inner.write_to(writer)

    @inline(.never)
    def write_repr_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the strided slice's debug representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        self._inner.write_repr_to(writer)

    def indices(self, length: Int) -> Tuple[Int, Int, Int]:
        """Resolves the slice's bounds against the length of a container.

        Bounds resolve with the same rules as `Slice.indices()`.

        Args:
            length: The length of the container the slice applies to.

        Returns:
            A tuple of the resolved start, end, and step.
        """
        return self._inner.indices(length)


struct ContiguousSlice(ImplicitlyCopyable, Writable):
    """Represents a slice expression without a stride.

    This type is used to support different behavior for strided vs unstrided
    slicing.
    """

    var start: Optional[Int]
    """The starting index of the slice."""
    var end: Optional[Int]
    """The end index of the slice."""

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(
        out self,
        start: Optional[Int],
        end: Optional[Int],
        stride: NoneType,
        __slice_literal__: NoneType = None,
    ):
        """Constructs a contiguous slice with the given start and end.

        Args:
            start: The starting index of the slice.
            end: The end index of the slice.
            stride: Always none. Disambiguates from slices with a stride.
            __slice_literal__: Enables slice literal syntax.
        """
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#
    # Trait implementations
    # ===-------------------------------------------------------------------===#

    @inline(.never)
    def write_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the contiguous slice's string representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        Slice(self.start, self.end, None).write_to(writer)

    @inline(.never)
    def write_repr_to(self, mut writer: Some[Writer]):
        """Writes the contiguous slice's debug representation to a writer.

        Args:
            writer: The object to write to.
        """
        Slice(self.start, self.end, None).write_repr_to(writer)

    def indices(self, length: Int) -> Tuple[Int, Int]:
        """Resolves the slice's start and end against the length of a
        container.

        A negative bound counts back from `length`, a `None` bound becomes
        the start or the end, and an out-of-bounds bound is clamped to the
        range `[0, length]`.

        Args:
            length: The length of the container the slice applies to.

        Returns:
            A tuple of the resolved start and end.
        """
        var start = self.start.or_else(0)
        var end = self.end.or_else(length)
        if start < 0:
            start = max(start + length, 0)
        elif start >= length:
            start = length

        if end < 0:
            end = max(end + length, 0)
        elif end >= length:
            end = length

        return start, end


# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#
# Slice constructor functions
# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#


@inline(.always)
def slice(end: Int) -> Slice:
    """Constructs a slice from the beginning up to `end`.

    A `Slice` holds the bounds that bracket slice syntax like `lst[1:5]`
    expresses. Constructing one directly is useful when the bounds are
    computed at run time. The end bound is exclusive.

    `indices()` resolves the bound against a container's length and counts a
    negative bound back from the end. Subscripting without a step is stricter:
    its bounds must be non-negative, and `lst[:-1]` aborts when bounds
    checking is enabled (the default on CPU) and causes undefined behavior
    otherwise. Compute the bound from the container's length instead, like
    `lst[: len(lst) - 1]` to stop one element short of the end.

    Args:
        end: The exclusive upper bound.

    Returns:
        A `Slice` covering the indices `0` up to `end`.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    var numbers: List[Int] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
    var from_start = slice(3)
    print(numbers[from_start])  # [10, 20, 30]
    print(from_start.indices(5))  # (0, 3, 1)
    ```
    """
    return Slice(None, end, None)


@inline(.always)
def slice(start: Int, end: Int) -> Slice:
    """Constructs a slice from `start` up to `end`.

    The bounds are half-open: the slice covers `start` up to, but not
    including, `end`. `indices()` resolves the bounds against a container's
    length and counts negative bounds back from the end. Subscripting without
    a step is stricter: its bounds must be non-negative, and `lst[1:-1]`
    aborts when bounds checking is enabled (the default on CPU) and causes
    undefined behavior otherwise. Compute bounds from the container's length
    instead, like `lst[1 : len(lst) - 1]` to stop one element short of the end.

    Args:
        start: The inclusive lower bound.
        end: The exclusive upper bound.

    Returns:
        A `Slice` covering the indices `start` up to `end`.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    var numbers: List[Int] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
    var s = slice(1, len(numbers) - 1)

    # Slicing the list copies the covered elements into a new list.
    var middle = numbers[s]
    print(middle)  # [20, 30, 40]

    # The bounds also resolve on their own, without a container.
    print(s.indices(len(numbers)))  # (1, 4, 1)
    ```
    """
    return Slice(start, end)


@inline(.always)
def slice(
    start: Optional[Int], end: Optional[Int], step: Optional[Int]
) -> Slice:
    """Constructs a slice from `start` to `end` stepping by `step`.

    The bounds are half-open. A `None` bound means the beginning or the end
    of the container, in the direction the step moves, and a `None` step
    means 1. `indices()` resolves the bounds against a container's length
    and counts negative bounds back from the end. Step-less slicing doesn't
    resolve negatives: its bounds must be non-negative, so compute them from
    the container's length instead.

    Args:
        start: The inclusive lower bound, or `None` for the beginning in
            the step's direction.
        end: The exclusive upper bound, or `None` for the end in the step's
            direction.
        step: The stride between the covered indices, where `None` means 1.

    Returns:
        A `Slice` covering the indices `start` to `end` by `step`.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    var numbers: List[Int] = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
    var backwards = slice(None, None, -1)
    print(numbers[backwards])  # [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
    print(backwards.indices(5))  # (4, -1, -1)
    ```
    """
    return Slice(start, end, step)

"""The runtime half of `__enum`: the compiler declares an enum's members
against this module, and nothing in it is user-facing.

For

```mojo
__enum Token:
    case eof
    case ident(String)
    case span(Int, Int)
```

the compiler generates, written as Mojo:

```mojo
struct Token(__Enum):
    comptime _enum_case_names = ["eof", "ident", "span"]
    comptime _enum_case_types = [NoneType, String, Tuple[Int, Int]]
    var __enum_storage: __EnumStorage[NoneType, String, Tuple[Int, Int]]

    comptime eof: Token = Token.__enum_init[0, NoneType]()

    @staticmethod
    def ident(var payload: String) -> Token:
        return Token.__enum_init[1, String](payload^)

    @staticmethod
    def span(var payload0: Int, var payload1: Int) -> Token:
        return Token.__enum_init[2, Tuple[Int, Int]](payload0^, payload1^)
```

`__EnumStorage` holds the active case's payload and its index, and copies,
moves and destroys the payload; the enum's own copy, move and destructor are
the ordinary struct ones over that single field. `__Enum`, a trait refining
`EnumLike`, supplies everything else as defaults: `__get_enum_storage` reaches
the field, `__enum_init` builds the value of a case, and the two `EnumLike`
methods read the field. The compiler finds these declarations by module
path.
"""

from std.builtin.enum_like import EnumLike
from std.builtin.variadics import TypeList, _MLIR
from std.sys import align_of, size_of
from std.traits import (
    IsTriviallyCopyable,
    IsTriviallyDeinitable,
    IsTriviallyMovable,
)


@doc_hidden
def __enum_discriminant_dtype(num_cases: Int) -> DType:
    """Returns the `!kgen.variant` discriminant type for `num_cases` cases."""
    if num_cases <= 256:
        return DType.uint8
    if num_cases <= 65536:
        return DType.uint16
    return DType.uint32


@doc_hidden
def __enum_payload_consists_of[Case: AnyType, *Ts: Movable]() -> Bool:
    """Returns whether elements of types `Ts` build a payload of type `Case`:
    the elements of a `Tuple`, the value itself for one payload type, nothing
    for `NoneType`."""
    # TODO(MOCO-5080): becomes `Case == Tuple[*Ts]`.
    comptime if Ts.length == 0:
        return Case == NoneType
    elif Ts.length == 1:
        return Case == Ts[0] or Case == Tuple[*Ts]
    else:
        return Case == Tuple[*Ts]


# TODO(MOCO-5080): `EnumLike` marks a case without a payload by using `NoneType`
# as its payload type, so `case_types` does the same. The marker goes away once
# every payload is a `Tuple`, `Tuple[]` for a case without one.
@doc_hidden
struct __EnumStorage[case_types: _MLIR.KGENParamListType[AnyType]](
    Copyable where TypeList[Trait=AnyType, case_types].all_conforms_to[
        Copyable
    ](),
    Deinitable where TypeList[Trait=AnyType, case_types].all_conforms_to[
        Deinitable
    ](),
    ImplicitlyCopyable where TypeList[
        Trait=AnyType, case_types
    ].all_conforms_to[ImplicitlyCopyable](),
    Movable where TypeList[Trait=AnyType, case_types].all_conforms_to[
        Movable
    ](),
    RegisterPassable where TypeList[Trait=AnyType, case_types].all_conforms_to[
        RegisterPassable
    ](),
):
    """The storage of an `__enum`: the payload of its active case and the index
    of that case.

    Cases are identified by index rather than by payload type, so several cases
    may share a payload type.

    Parameters:
        case_types: The payload type of each case, `NoneType` for a case without
            a payload.
    """

    comptime _Cases = TypeList[Trait=AnyType, Self.case_types]

    comptime __del__is_trivial = Self._Cases.all[IsTriviallyDeinitable]()
    comptime __copy_ctor_is_trivial = Self._Cases.all[IsTriviallyCopyable]()
    comptime __move_ctor_is_trivial = Self._Cases.all[IsTriviallyMovable]()

    comptime _mlir_type = __mlir_type[
        `!kgen.variant<[rebind(:`,
        type_of(Self.case_types),
        ` `,
        Self.case_types,
        `)]>`,
    ]
    var _impl: Self._mlir_type

    # Build discriminants with `from_int=`, a plain `pop.cast`. Declaring an
    # enum resolves its copy constructor, and a conversion through `SIMD.cast`
    # there would pull in `String` and the atomics, so an enum could not
    # appear in the signature of anything those depend on.
    comptime _Discriminant = Scalar[
        __enum_discriminant_dtype(Self._Cases.length)
    ]

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(out self, *, unsafe_uninitialized: Tuple[]):
        __mlir_op.`lit.ownership.mark_initialized`(__get_mvalue_as_litref(self))

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(
        out self, *, copy: Self
    ) where Self._Cases.all_conforms_to[Copyable]():
        comptime if Self.__copy_ctor_is_trivial:
            self._impl = copy._impl
            return
        self = Self(unsafe_uninitialized=())
        var discriminant = copy._discriminant()
        self._discriminant() = discriminant
        comptime for i in range(Self._Cases.length):
            # The `where` clause states the constraint; the solver does not
            # derive the element's conformance from `all_conforms_to`, so the
            # assert supplies it for the call below (as in `Tuple.__init__`).
            comptime assert conforms_to(Self._Cases()[i], Copyable)
            if discriminant == Self._Discriminant(from_int=i):
                self.payload_ptr[i]().unsafe_write(copy=copy.payload_ptr[i]()[])

    @inline(.always)
    def __init__(
        out self, *, deinit move: Self
    ) where Self._Cases.all_conforms_to[Movable]():
        comptime if Self.__move_ctor_is_trivial:
            self._impl = move._impl
            return
        self = Self(unsafe_uninitialized=())
        var discriminant = move._discriminant()
        self._discriminant() = discriminant
        comptime for i in range(Self._Cases.length):
            comptime assert conforms_to(Self._Cases()[i], Movable)
            if discriminant == Self._Discriminant(from_int=i):
                self.payload_ptr[i]().unsafe_write_move_from(
                    move.payload_ptr[i]()
                )

    @inline(.always)
    def __deinit__(deinit self) where Self._Cases.all_conforms_to[Deinitable]():
        var discriminant = self._discriminant()
        comptime for i in range(Self._Cases.length):
            comptime assert conforms_to(Self._Cases()[i], Deinitable)
            if discriminant == Self._Discriminant(from_int=i):
                self.payload_ptr[i]().unsafe_deinit_pointee()

    @inline(.nodebug)
    def _discriminant(ref self) -> ref[self] Self._Discriminant:
        var discr_ptr = __mlir_op.`pop.variant.discr_gep`[
            _type=__mlir_type[
                `!kgen.pointer<scalar<`,
                Self._Discriminant.dtype._mlir_value,
                `>>`,
            ]
        ](Pointer(to=self._impl)._get_kgen_pointer())
        return Pointer[_, origin_of(self)](
            _mlir_value=discr_ptr
        ).unsafe_bitcast[Self._Discriminant]()[]

    @inline(.nodebug)
    def get_discriminant(self) -> Int:
        """Returns the index of the active case.

        Returns:
            The index of the active case.
        """
        return Int(mlir_value=self._discriminant().__mlir_index__())

    @inline(.nodebug)
    def payload_ptr[
        id: Int
    ](ref self) -> Pointer[Self._Cases()[id], origin_of(self)]:
        """Returns a pointer to the payload of case `id`.

        Only valid when case `id` is active.

        Parameters:
            id: The index of the case.

        Returns:
            A pointer to the payload of case `id`.
        """
        return {
            _mlir_value = __mlir_op.`pop.variant.bitcast`[
                _type=Pointer[Self._Cases()[id], origin_of(self)]._mlir_type,
                index=id.__mlir_index__(),
            ](Pointer(to=self._impl)._get_kgen_pointer())
        }


trait __Enum(EnumLike):
    """An `__enum`: a struct whose only field, `__enum_storage`, is an
    `__EnumStorage` over its case types. `__get_enum_storage` reaches that
    field; the two `EnumLike` methods read it and `__enum_init` writes it."""

    @inline(.always)
    def __get_enum_storage(
        ref self,
    ) -> ref[self] __EnumStorage[Self._enum_case_types]:
        """Returns the storage field, the enum's only field."""
        comptime Storage = __EnumStorage[Self._enum_case_types]
        comptime assert (
            size_of[Self]() == size_of[Storage]()
            and align_of[Self]() == align_of[Storage]()
        ), "an `__Enum` must have its storage as its only field"
        # A cast, not a field access: a register-passable enum is lowered as
        # its storage itself, and a field access on the generic `Self` relies
        # on the compiler folding it away for such an enum.
        return Pointer(to=self).unsafe_bitcast[Storage]()[]

    @staticmethod
    @inline(.always)
    def __enum_init[
        id: Int, Case: AnyType, *Ts: Movable
    ](var *payload: *Ts, out result: Self):
        """Constructs the value of case `id`, whose payload type is `Case`,
        from the payload's elements: nothing for a case without one, the
        value for a single payload type, the elements of the `Tuple` for
        several. Each one is written straight into the storage."""
        comptime Storage = __EnumStorage[Self._enum_case_types]
        # The compiler binds `id`, `Case` and `Ts` from the case it emits
        # the call for; a hand-written call is checked the same way.
        comptime assert (
            0 <= id < Storage._Cases.length
        ), "case index must be below the case count"
        comptime assert (
            Case == Storage._Cases()[id]
        ), "payload type must be the case's payload type"
        comptime assert __enum_payload_consists_of[
            Case, *Ts
        ](), "payload elements must build the case's payload type"
        # The payload arrives as a pack and each element is written into the
        # storage where it will live, instead of being gathered into one
        # payload value that is then moved in as a whole. That would move each
        # element twice, into the value and then with it into the storage, and
        # the second move survives for a move constructor with effects and in
        # unoptimized builds. The element types cannot be spelled from `Case`,
        # since a pack's types must be a variadic parameter, so `Ts` is a
        # parameter of its own, inferred from the arguments the synthesized
        # case member passes on unchanged.
        # The result is built in place: its storage is created uninitialized
        # and given the discriminant, then the payload slot is filled.
        __mlir_op.`lit.ownership.mark_initialized`(
            __get_mvalue_as_litref(result)
        )
        var storage = Pointer(to=result.__get_enum_storage())
        __get_address_as_uninit_lvalue(storage._mlir_value) = Storage(
            unsafe_uninitialized=()
        )
        storage[]._discriminant() = Storage._Discriminant(from_int=id)
        var slot = storage[].payload_ptr[id]()

        # `slot` is typed by the case type, which the type checker cannot
        # relate to `Ts`, hence the bitcast in each branch. The branches exist
        # because the case type depends on the element count today: a `Tuple`
        # for several elements, the element type itself for one, `NoneType`
        # for none. TODO(MOCO-5080): once every payload is a `Tuple`, only the
        # first branch remains (with its bitcast, and `Ts` as a parameter: a
        # pack's element types must be a variadic parameter, so they cannot
        # be read off the case type); it is first so that `Tuple[T]` and
        # `Tuple[]` already take it.
        comptime if Case == Tuple[*Ts]:
            # The tuple never exists as a separate value: each element goes
            # into its place inside the slot, as `Tuple.__init__` fills its
            # own storage.
            var elements = slot.unsafe_bitcast[Tuple[*Ts]]()

            def init_element[i: Int](var element: Ts[i]) {elements}:
                Pointer(to=elements[][i]).unsafe_write(element^)

            payload^.consume_elements(init_element)
        elif Ts.length == 1:

            def init_value[i: Int](var value: Ts[i]) {slot}:
                slot.unsafe_bitcast[Ts[i]]().unsafe_write(value^)

            payload^.consume_elements(init_value)
        else:
            slot.unsafe_bitcast[NoneType]().unsafe_write(None)

    @inline(.always)
    def _get_enum_discriminant(self) -> Int:
        return self.__get_enum_storage().get_discriminant()

    @inline(.always)
    def _unsafe_get_enum_payload[
        id: Int
    ](ref self) -> ref[self] TypeList[Trait=AnyType, Self._enum_case_types]()[
        id
    ]:
        return self.__get_enum_storage().payload_ptr[id]()[]

"""Provides the `bin`, `hex`, and `oct` functions.

These are Mojo built-ins, so you don't need to import them.
"""

from std.sys import bit_width_of

comptime _DEFAULT_DIGIT_CHARS = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"


# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#
# bin
# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#


def bin(num: Scalar, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0b") -> String:
    """Returns the binary string representation of an integer.

    The string is prefixed with `"0b"` by default. Negative values start
    with a minus sign, like `-0b1111011`.

    Args:
        num: The integer value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0b"`).

    Returns:
        The binary string representation of the integer.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    print(bin(123))  # 0b1111011
    print(bin(-123))  # -0b1111011
    print(bin(123, prefix=""))  # 1111011
    ```
    """
    return _format_int[radix=2](num, prefix=prefix)


# Need this until we have constraints to stop the compiler from matching this
# directly to bin[dtype: DType](num: Scalar[dtype]).
def bin(b: Scalar[.bool], /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0b") -> String:
    """Returns the binary string representation of a bool value.

    The bool is formatted as an integer, so the result is `0b0` or `0b1`
    with the default prefix.

    Args:
        b: The bool value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0b"`).

    Returns:
        The binary string representation of the bool.
    """
    return bin(b.cast[.int8](), prefix=prefix)


def bin[T: Intable, //](num: T, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0b") -> String:
    """Returns the binary string representation of a value.

    The value is converted to `Int` and formatted in base 2, prefixed with
    `"0b"` by default.

    Parameters:
        T: The type of the value. Must conform to `Intable`.

    Args:
        num: The value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0b"`).

    Returns:
        The binary string representation of the value.
    """
    return bin(Int(Int(num)), prefix=prefix)


# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#
# hex
# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#


def hex(value: Scalar, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0x") -> String:
    """Returns the hexadecimal string representation of an integer.

    The string is prefixed with `"0x"` by default and uses lowercase digits.
    Negative values start with a minus sign, like `-0xff`.

    Args:
        value: The integer value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0x"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the hexadecimal representation of the value.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    print(hex(255))  # 0xff
    print(hex(-255))  # -0xff
    print(hex(255, prefix=""))  # ff
    ```
    """
    return _format_int[radix=16](value, prefix=prefix)


def hex[T: Intable, //](value: T, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0x") -> String:
    """Returns the hexadecimal string representation of a value.

    The value is converted to `Int` and formatted in base 16, prefixed with
    `"0x"` by default.

    Parameters:
        T: The type of the value. Must conform to `Intable`.

    Args:
        value: The value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0x"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the hexadecimal representation of the value.
    """
    return hex(Int(Int(value)), prefix=prefix)


def hex(value: Scalar[.bool], /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0x") -> String:
    """Returns the hexadecimal string representation of a bool value.

    The bool is formatted as an integer, so the result is `0x0` or `0x1`
    with the default prefix.

    Args:
        value: The bool value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0x"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the hexadecimal representation of the bool.
    """
    return hex(value.cast[.int8](), prefix=prefix)


# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#
# oct
# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#


def oct(value: Scalar, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0o") -> String:
    """Returns the octal string representation of an integer.

    The string is prefixed with `"0o"` by default. Negative values start
    with a minus sign, like `-0o173`.

    Args:
        value: The integer value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0o"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the octal representation of the value.

    For example:

    ```mojo
    print(oct(64))  # 0o100
    print(oct(-123))  # -0o173
    print(oct(64, prefix=""))  # 100
    ```
    """
    return _format_int[radix=8](value, prefix=prefix)


def oct[T: Intable, //](value: T, /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0o") -> String:
    """Returns the octal string representation of a value.

    The value is converted to `Int` and formatted in base 8, prefixed with
    `"0o"` by default.

    Parameters:
        T: The type of the value. Must conform to `Intable`.

    Args:
        value: The value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0o"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the octal representation of the value.
    """
    return oct(Int(Int(value)), prefix=prefix)


def oct(value: Scalar[.bool], /, *, prefix: StaticString = "0o") -> String:
    """Returns the octal string representation of a bool value.

    The bool is formatted as an integer, so the result is `0o0` or `0o1`
    with the default prefix.

    Args:
        value: The bool value to format.
        prefix: The prefix prepended to the digits (defaults to `"0o"`).

    Returns:
        A string containing the octal representation of the bool.
    """
    return oct(value.cast[.int8](), prefix=prefix)


# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#
# Integer formatting utilities
# ===-----------------------------------------------------------------------===#


def _format_int[
    dtype: DType,
    *,
    radix: Int = 10,
    digit_chars: StaticString = _DEFAULT_DIGIT_CHARS,
](value: Scalar[dtype], *, prefix: StaticString = "",) -> String:
    var output = String()
    _write_int[radix=radix, digit_chars=digit_chars](
        output, value, prefix=prefix
    )
    return output^


def _write_int[
    dtype: DType,
    W: Writer,
    //,
    *,
    radix: Int = 10,
    digit_chars: StaticString = _DEFAULT_DIGIT_CHARS,
](mut writer: W, value: Scalar[dtype], *, prefix: StaticString = "",):
    """Writes a formatted string representation of the given integer using the
    specified radix.

    The maximum supported radix is 36 unless a custom `digit_chars` mapping is
    provided.
    """
    comptime assert dtype.is_integral(), "Expected integral"
    comptime assert (
        radix >= 2
    ), "Unable to format integer to string with radix < 2"
    comptime assert radix <= digit_chars.byte_length(), (
        "Unable to format integer to string when provided radix is larger than"
        " length of available digit value characters"
    )
    comptime assert digit_chars.byte_length() >= 2, (
        "Unable to format integer to string when provided digit_chars mapping"
        " len is not >= 2"
    )

    # Process the integer value into its corresponding digits

    # TODO(#26444, Unicode support): Get an array of Character, not bytes.
    var digit_chars_array = digit_chars.as_bytes()

    # Prefix a '-' if the original int was negative and make positive.
    if value < 0:
        writer.write_string("-")

    # Add the custom number prefix, e.g. "0x" commonly used for hex numbers.
    # This comes *after* the minus sign, if present.
    writer.write(prefix)

    if value == 0:
        # TODO: Replace with safe digit_chars[:1] syntax.
        # SAFETY:
        #   This static origin is valid as long as we're using a
        #   `StaticString` for `digit_chars`.
        var zero_char = digit_chars_array.unsafe_ptr()[]

        # Construct a null-terminated buffer of single-byte char.
        var zero_buf: Array[UInt8, 2] = [zero_char, 0]

        # TODO(MSTDL-720):
        #   Support printing non-null-terminated strings on GPU and switch
        #   back to this code without a workaround.
        # ptr=digit_chars_array,
        writer.write(
            StringSpan(
                unsafe_from_utf8=Span(
                    unsafe_ptr=zero_buf.unsafe_ptr(), length=1
                )
            )
        )

        return

    # Create a buffer to store the formatted value

    # Stack allocate enough bytes to store any formatted integer up to 256 bits
    # TODO: use a dynamic size when #2194 is resolved
    # +1 for storing NUL terminator.
    comptime CAPACITY: Int = max(64, bit_width_of[dtype]()) + 1

    var buf = Array[UInt8, CAPACITY](uninitialized=True)

    # Start the buf pointer at the end. We will write the least-significant
    # digits later in the buffer, and then decrement the pointer to move
    # earlier in the buffer as we write the more-significant digits.
    var offset = CAPACITY - 1

    buf.unsafe_ptr().unsafe_offset(offset).write(
        0
    )  # Write NUL terminator at the end

    # Position the offset to write the least-significant digit just before the
    # NUL terminator.
    offset -= 1

    # Write the digits of the number
    var remaining_int = value

    def process_digits[
        get_digit_value: def(Scalar[dtype]) thin -> Scalar[dtype],
        div_fn: def(Scalar[dtype]) thin -> Scalar[dtype],
    ]() {mut}:
        while remaining_int:
            var digit_value = get_digit_value(remaining_int)

            # Write the char representing the value of the least significant
            # digit.
            buf.unsafe_ptr().unsafe_offset(offset).write(
                digit_chars_array.unsafe_ptr()[unsafe_offset=Int(digit_value)]
            )

            # Position the offset to write the next digit.
            offset -= 1

            # TODO: (MOCO-3028)
            # We should be able to simply do `remaining_int /= radix` here,
            # however, there is a compiler bug when using `/` in parameter
            # vs argument for signed SIMD values.
            #
            # Drop the least significant digit
            remaining_int = div_fn(remaining_int)

    if remaining_int >= 0:

        def pos_digit_value(value: Scalar[dtype]) -> Scalar[dtype]:
            return value % Scalar[dtype](radix)

        def floor_div(value: Scalar[dtype]) -> Scalar[dtype]:
            return value / Scalar[dtype](radix)

        process_digits[pos_digit_value, floor_div]()
    else:

        def neg_digit_value(value: Scalar[dtype]) -> Scalar[dtype]:
            return abs(value % Scalar[dtype](-radix))

        def ceil_div(value: Scalar[dtype]) -> Scalar[dtype]:
            return value.__ceildiv__(Scalar[dtype](radix))

        process_digits[neg_digit_value, ceil_div]()

    # Re-add +1 byte since the loop ended so we didn't write another char.
    offset += 1

    # Create a span to only those bytes in `buf` that have been initialized.
    # -1 because NUL terminator
    writer.write_string(
        StringSpan(
            unsafe_from_utf8=Span(
                unsafe_ptr=buf.unsafe_ptr().unsafe_offset(offset),
                length=len(buf) - offset - 1,
            )
        )
    )
